q1: I would start an empiric, CNS-penetrant alkylating chemotherapy now rather than wait, while being explicit that this is not disease-specific therapy because the entity is still unclassified. The most reasonable choice is single-agent oral temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2 on days 1-5 every 28 days): it penetrates the CNS, is generally well tolerated, and has activity in high-grade gliomas and other high-grade CNS tumors; this is also what the patient has now started. Reasonable alternatives are a nitrosourea such as lomustine (130 mg/m2 every 6 weeks) or PCV if a glioma-like biology is suspected. If the tumor were later shown to behave as an extracranial-type soft-tissue sarcoma, an anthracycline/ifosfamide- or gemcitabine/docetaxel-based regimen could be discussed, but those drugs have poor CNS penetration and substantial toxicity, so I would not choose them empirically for brain-dominant disease. I would obtain informed consent, document the diagnostic uncertainty, arrange early contrast MRI re-assessment, and continue tissue/molecular workup and clinical-trial screening in parallel. Bevacizumab is not chemotherapy, but it could be considered later for radiation necrosis/edema or as a palliative anti-angiogenic option, not as definitive therapy.
q2: No, I would not routinely add a second cytotoxic drug at this point. The entity remains unclassified, there is no evidence that any combination improves survival in this disease, and the patient is tolerating single-agent temozolomide without significant toxicity. The best-studied add-on in high-grade glioma is lomustine (EORTC 26101 showed improved progression-free survival but no overall survival benefit and more toxicity); PCV adds myelosuppression and alopecia without a clear advantage over temozolomide, and sarcoma-type combinations add toxicity without proven CNS benefit. I would continue single-agent temozolomide, reassess with contrast MRI after 2-3 cycles, and revisit combination therapy only if the diagnosis becomes established (for example, a confirmed high-grade glioma or sarcoma), if there is clear progression, or within a clinical trial. If a second drug were required later, lomustine would be the most defensible partner, but that decision should be individualized and not made empirically today.
q3: No. I would not stop temozolomide and switch to an FGFR2-directed agent on the basis of a plasma ctDNA report alone. First, liquid biopsy in primary CNS disease can have low tumor fraction and is prone to false-positive and false-negative results; a fusion call, especially alongside other alterations, needs orthogonal tissue confirmation with an RNA-based fusion panel, FGFR2 immunohistochemistry/FISH, and review of the resected tumor. Second, the histologic entity remains unestablished; this molecular profile does not establish a diagnosis, and the FGFR2 fusion may be passenger or subclonal rather than the driver. Third, the accompanying KRAS, STK11 and CTNNB1 alterations have no validated single-target therapy in this context and could indicate resistance or a different tumor biology. Fourth, there is no approved FGFR2-targeted therapy for an unclassified intracranial mesenchymal neoplasm, and available FGFR inhibitors have limited CNS data and penetration. My plan is to continue temozolomide, send the archival resection tissue for confirmatory comprehensive profiling including RNA fusion analysis and FGFR2 immunohistochemistry/FISH, and present the case at a molecular tumor board. Only if tissue confirms a clonal, actionable FGFR2 fusion, and preferably within a clinical trial or after explicit multidisciplinary and off-label consent, would I consider an FGFR inhibitor; otherwise I would not abandon chemotherapy for an unproven target. I would continue imaging surveillance and supportive care.
